title: Chinese Spare Ribs with Black Bean
subtitle: pork spare ribs braised with fermented black beans and garlic
excerpt: Meaty spare ribs braised low and slow with fermented black beans, garlic, ginger and a splash of Shaoxing wine until autumn-off-the-bone tender. A Cantonese classic ready in about an hour. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Black bean spare ribs are a cornerstone of Cantonese cooking and appear across dim sum menus and home kitchens throughout Guangdong, Hong Kong and the Cantonese diaspora. The combination of fermented black beans with pork is ancient, referenced in Chinese culinary texts from the Han dynasty onward. Modern home recipes are documented in Cantonese cookbooks throughout the twentieth century. The braised version differs from the steamed dim sum preparation in using a clay pot or heavy pan to build deeper flavour.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked ribs in their sauce for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The ribs taste better the day after cooking. Reheat gently with a splash of water or stock.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small black soy beans that have been salted and fermented until intensely savoury and slightly funky. They are sold dried or in jars. Rinse before using to reduce saltiness and roughly chop or crush to release their flavour.
A fermented paste made from broad beans and chillies, central to Sichuan cooking. It is salty, spicy and deeply savoury. Pixian county doubanjiang is considered the finest variety.
A Chinese rice wine with a nutty, amber flavour used widely in marinades, sauces and braises. Named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. Dry sherry is the closest substitute.

content.text: These ribs take about 60 minutes and serve 4. Spare ribs are marinated briefly then braised with
fermented black beans
, garlic, ginger,
Shaoxing wine
and a small amount of
doubanjiang
for depth. The sauce reduces to a glossy coating.
Rinse the fermented black beans and give them a rough chop before adding. Whole beans stay intact and give uneven bursts of flavour; chopped beans distribute into the sauce more evenly.
What you need

items.prepNote: cut into 5 cm pieces, ask the butcher to do this

content.text: Method
Toss the ribs with 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp light soy sauce and a pinch of white pepper. Leave to marinate for 15 minutes.
Heat the oil in a wok or heavy casserole over high heat. Brown the ribs in batches for 2 to 3 minutes per side. Remove and set aside.
Reduce heat to medium. Add the garlic, ginger and fermented black beans. Stir-fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the doubanjiang and stir for 30 seconds.
Return the ribs to the pan. Add the remaining 2 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp light soy, dark soy, sugar and chicken stock. Stir to combine.
Bring to the boil, then reduce to a low simmer. Cover and cook for 30 minutes, turning the ribs once halfway through.
Uncover and cook for a further 10 minutes over medium heat, turning the ribs in the sauce until it has reduced to a glaze.
Scatter over spring onions and serve with steamed rice.

items.symptom: Ribs are still tough after 30 minutes
items.cause: The braise temperature was too low, or the ribs were thick.
items.fix: Make sure the liquid is at a gentle but active simmer, not just warm. Add 10 more minutes of covered cooking if needed.

items.cause: Black beans, soy sauce and doubanjiang are all salt-heavy.
items.fix: Reduce or omit the dark soy and taste before adding any more light soy.
Remove the lid and boil for a few extra minutes, turning the ribs to coat them as the sauce reduces.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Black bean spare ribs are a pillar of Cantonese cooking, appearing in both the braised form described here and as a lighter steamed dim sum version. Cantonese cooks have paired fermented black beans with pork for a very long time, using the beans' intense umami to elevate otherwise simple cuts. The dish travels well: it tastes even better the next day, making it a practical choice for home cooking.
